title: Open Problem: Expansion vs. Corruption Detection
statement_text: There is still a significant gap between the expansion properties that suffice for solving the corruption detection problem (strong spectral expansion, as in Ramanujan graphs) and the necessary condition that the graph cannot be split into components of size at most $\epsilon n$ by removing at most $\epsilon n$ vertices. It will be interesting to obtain tighter relations between expansion and corruption detection.
context_text: In the corruption detection problem, each vertex (agent) of a graph $G$ on $n$ vertices is either truthful or corrupt; every truthful vertex reports the true type of each of its neighbours, while corrupt vertices may report arbitrarily (and collude). From the reports, one wants to identify with certainty the types of as many vertices as possible, assuming a majority $|T|>|B|$ of truthful vertices (otherwise nothing can be identified). An $(n,d,\lambda)$-graph is a $d$-regular $n$-vertex graph whose eigenvalues other than the largest have absolute value at most $\lambda$; it is Ramanujan if $\lambda\le2\sqrt{d-1}$. The authors prove that for a Ramanujan $(n,d,\lambda)$-graph with $d\ge100$ one can, from any report compatible with a truthful majority, identify all but at most $\frac{32}{d}|B|$ truthful and all but $\frac{32}{d}|B|$ corrupt vertices (in linear time if $|T|>(1+\frac{12}{d})\frac n2$, while the problem is NP-hard for a bare majority even on expanders). Conversely, if removing at most $\epsilon n$ vertices leaves only components of size at most $\epsilon n$, then even with $|T|\ge(1-2\epsilon)n$ no truthful vertex can be identified (e.g. planar or minor-free graphs with $\epsilon=\Theta(n^{-1/3})$). In the concluding discussion the authors ask for sharp criteria, in terms of expansion and the fraction $|T|/n$, enabling corruption detection, and give a weak result: if $G$ is $\epsilon$-connected (every two disjoint sets of sizes at least $\epsilon n$ and $(1-3\epsilon)n$ are joined by an edge) and $|T|=(1-\epsilon)n$, then a subset of $T$ of size at least $(1-2\epsilon)n$ can be identified, which is tight up to constants. A follow-up work relates the question to the Small Set Expansion hypothesis.
